newsitem.title: INDIA: India hails trade win over U.S., swears by WTO.
newsitem.headline: India hails trade win over U.S., swears by WTO.

text.p: India, lauding a World Trade Organisation (WTO) decision to strike down a U.S. curb on woollen exports from India, said on Saturday that New Delhi will not hesitate to approach WTO if it suspects foul play on trade.

"When they (United States) wanted to do it (curb wool exports from India), WTO said: 'You are wrong. You can't do it'," Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah told an international business conference in Calcutta.
A WTO panel last month found the United States violated free trade rules by slapping limits last year on imports of some woollen clothing from India.

The import restrictions, which affected woven men's shirts and women's blouses, were introduced from April 1995 after the United States said a surge of these goods from India posed a threat of serious damage to domestic producers.
The restrictions were extended for another 12 months in April last year but were withdrawn in December after U.S. officials said there had been a steady decline in imports.

India took the case, together with a linked complaint on U.S. limits imposed on woollen coats, to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body after another WTO body, the Textile Monitoring Board, effectively sanctioned the U.S. move.
Indian officials argued that the unilateral restrictions ran against the 1994 world trade treaty and its Agreement on Textiles and Clothing.
Ramaiah's remarks were in sharp contrast to New Delhi's initial reaction to India's victory, which was discreet silence.
He defended India's decision to join the WTO, which had faced criticism from leftist groups and opposition lawmakers.
"I have the leverage," the minister said. "Don't think we are going to surrender to anybody."
Ramaiah said India wanted to go ahead with its plans to gradually reduce import tariffs.
He said India could also use anti-dumping provisions to defend itself against unfair trade.
Anti-dumping duties are imposed by a country if it feels that imports from another country are at prices below the costs at which they are manufactured.
Ramaiah said New Delhi wanted to join an agreement signed at the WTO's ministerial meeting in Singapore last month. The pact seeks to eliminate import duties on information technology goods by 2000.

"We are very keen on it. We do have an advantage in it," Ramaiah said."But my electronics department said on some things they wanted more time (to reduce tariffs). We have not rejected it. I have kept it on hold."
In response to a question, Ramaiah said high agricultural subsidies in some countries were hindering exports from developing countries, and added that India planned to approach the WTO on the issue.
"Subsidies offered by various countries are much more than what we are doing in this country," he said.
"At the next ministerial conference, we will certainly take up this issue," Ramaiah said. "We have to make more and more agricultural exports."
Developing countries have often criticised Western countries and Japan for subsidising their farm sectors.
